expectedText:
RESIDENTIAL LEASE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee

PARTIES AND PROPERTY
This is a residential lease agreement between Acme Properties, LLC ("Landlord") and Jordan Lee ("Tenant") for the property at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield. The lease term runs from September 1, 2026 to August 31, 2027.

RENT
Tenant will pay Landlord rent of $2,200 per month, due on the _______ day of each month, payable by: _______________________________________________.

SECURITY DEPOSIT
Landlord may charge a security deposit of up to one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent. If Landlord is an individual (or an LLC whose members are all individuals) who owns no more than two residential rental properties totaling no more than four units, Landlord may charge up to two months' rent instead — except that this higher cap doesn't apply if the prospective tenant is a service member, in which case the general one-month cap still controls. The deposit may only be used for: (1) unpaid rent; (2) repairing damage Tenant (or Tenant's guest) caused, beyond ordinary wear and tear; (3) cleaning needed to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in when the tenancy began; and (4) remedying a future default in returning or restoring personal property, if the lease authorizes that use. Within 21 days after Tenant moves out, Landlord must give Tenant an itemized statement of any deductions and return the remaining deposit.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, general security deposit cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to two months’ rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy if the landlord meets both of the following requirements: (i) The landlord is a natural person or a limited liability company in which all members are natural persons. (ii) The landlord owns no more than two residential rental properties that collectively include no more than four dwelling units offered for rent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(5)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, higher cap for a small individual landlord (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "Subparagraph (A) shall not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(5)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the small-landlord cap doesn't apply to a service-member tenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "This subdivision does not prohibit an advance payment of not less than six months’ rent if the term of the lease is six months or longer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, advance rent for a longer lease (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "(1) The compensation of a landlord for a tenant’s default in the payment of rent. (2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. (3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the four permitted uses of a security deposit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "(4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(b)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the fourth permitted use — future personal-property defaults (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, deposit return deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: A lease of six months or longer can separately require an advance rent payment of up to six months' rent, on top of the security deposit cap above — a different rule from the deposit cap itself, and easy to conflate with it. This is one state's statute, current as of a 2024 change that lowered the general cap to one month's rent; deposit limits and return deadlines vary by state, and this document doesn't track any state but this one. All six citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

TENANT'S RIGHT TO A PRE-MOVE-OUT INSPECTION
Before Tenant moves out, Landlord must notify Tenant in writing of Tenant's option to request an initial (pre-move-out) inspection and the right to be present for it. If Tenant requests one, Landlord must inspect no earlier than two weeks before the move-out date and give Tenant at least 48 hours' written notice of the inspection date and time. The point of this inspection is to let Tenant fix any identified problems before move-out, to avoid a deduction from the deposit for them.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. The purpose of the initial inspection shall be to allow the tenant an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies, in a manner consistent with the rights and obligations of the parties under the rental agreement, in order to avoid deductions from the security."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the pre-move-out inspection right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The landlord shall give at least 48 hours’ prior written notice of the date and time of the inspection if either a mutual time is agreed upon, or if a mutually agreed time cannot be scheduled but the tenant still wishes an inspection."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, 48-hour inspection notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "if an initial inspection is conducted pursuant to this subdivision and, at the time of inspection, the premises do not contain tenant possessions that prevent the landlord from identifying repairs or cleanings due to the presence of those possessions, the landlord shall not use the security for deductions for repairs or cleanings that are not identified in the itemized statement described in paragraph (2)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, effect of not identifying an issue at the inspection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The requirements of this subdivision do not apply when the tenancy is terminated pursuant to subdivision (2), (3), or (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(7) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, this right doesn't apply to a for-cause unlawful detainer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: If Tenant requests this inspection and the unit isn't full of Tenant's belongings in a way that would hide problems from view, Landlord generally can't later deduct from the deposit for a repair or cleaning issue that wasn't identified at that inspection. This is a real, concrete consequence of the inspection right, not just a formality — and it's easy to miss because the inspection itself is optional (Tenant has to request it; if Tenant doesn't, this whole process — and its protection — doesn't apply). This entire inspection right doesn't apply at all if the tenancy is ending through an unlawful detainer based on nonpayment of rent, a lease breach, or waste/nuisance — those specific for-cause terminations void the right described in this clause. This is one state's statute; not every state gives tenants this specific right. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

PHOTO DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENT
For a tenancy that begins on or after July 1, 2025, Landlord must photograph the unit before or at the start of the tenancy. Separately, beginning April 1, 2025, Landlord must photograph the unit after Tenant moves out but before making any repairs or cleaning charged against the deposit, and again after that repair or cleaning is finished.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "For tenancies that begin on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord shall take photographs of the unit immediately before, or at the inception of, the tenancy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, move-in photo requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord shall take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after the possession of the unit is returned to the landlord, but prior to any repairs or cleanings for which the landlord will make a deduction from or claim against the security deposit pursuant to this section, and shall also take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after such repairs or cleanings are completed."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, move-out before-and-after photo requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "If a deduction is made for repairs or cleanings allowed by this section, the landlord shall provide photographs taken pursuant to subdivision (g), along with a written explanation of the cost of the allowable repairs or cleanings, as described in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the photos are a required part of the deduction documentation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: This is a very recent requirement — it phases in on two different dates for two different purposes (a baseline record at move-in, and a before-and-after record around any move-out deduction) — and it's one state's statute, not a nationwide practice. The move-out photos aren't just good practice: for any deduction the landlord makes for repairs or cleaning, the statute separately requires the landlord to provide those same photographs to the tenant, along with a written explanation of the cost, as part of the itemized deduction statement — so skipping the photos leaves the landlord unable to fully comply with that separate documentation requirement. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

HABITABILITY
Landlord must maintain the property in a condition fit for human habitation and repair conditions that make it uninhabitable, except for conditions Tenant caused.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "The lessor of a building intended for the occupation of human beings must, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, put it into a condition fit for such occupation, and repair all subsequent dilapidations thereof, which render it untenantable, except such as are mentioned in section nineteen hundred and twenty-nine."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1941 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, landlord's habitability duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.)
  "Any agreement by a lessee of a dwelling waiving or modifying his rights under Section 1941 or 1942 shall be void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable, except that the lessor and the lessee may agree that the lessee shall undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.1 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, habitability duty can't be waived (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.1.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text says this duty applies "in the absence of an agreement to the contrary" — which could read as if a lease could waive it. A separate provision closes that door for residential tenancies: a lease clause waiving or modifying this duty is void as against public policy, for any condition that actually makes the unit uninhabitable. The one thing landlord and tenant can agree to instead is having the tenant handle some repairs or maintenance as part of the rental terms — that's different from waiving the underlying habitability duty altogether. This is one state's statute; habitability protections exist in some form in most states, but the details vary.

WHAT "HABITABLE" SPECIFICALLY MEANS
A unit is legally uninhabitable if it substantially lacks any of the following: effective weatherproofing (including intact windows and doors); working plumbing and gas fixtures that met the code in effect when installed; hot and cold running water connected to an approved sewage system; working heating that met the code in effect when installed; working electrical wiring and lighting that met the code in effect when installed; a building and grounds kept clean, sanitary, and free of debris, rodents, and vermin; adequate garbage and rubbish receptacles, kept in clean condition and good repair; and floors, stairways, and railings kept in good repair.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "A dwelling shall be deemed untenantable for purposes of Section 1941 if it substantially lacks any of the following affirmative standard characteristics or is a residential unit described in Section 17920.3 or 17920.10 of the Health and Safety Code: (1) Effective waterproofing and weather protection of roof and exterior walls, including unbroken windows and doors. (2) Plumbing or gas facilities that conformed to applicable law in effect at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (3) A water supply approved under applicable law that is under the control of the tenant, capable of producing hot and cold running water, or a system that is under the control of the landlord, that produces hot and cold running water, furnished to appropriate fixtures, and connected to a sewage disposal system approved under applicable law. (4) Heating facilities that conformed with applicable law at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (5) Electrical lighting, with wiring and electrical equipment that conformed with applicable law at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (6) Building, grounds, and appurtenances at the time of the commencement of the lease or rental agreement, and all areas under control of the landlord, kept in every part clean, sanitary, and free from all accumulations of debris, filth, rubbish, garbage, rodents, and vermin. (7) An adequate number of appropriate receptacles for garbage and rubbish, in clean condition and good repair at the time of the commencement of the lease or rental agreement, with the landlord providing appropriate serviceable receptacles thereafter and being responsible for the clean condition and good repair of the receptacles under their control. (8) Floors, stairways, and railings maintained in good repair."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(1)-(8) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the specific tenantability checklist (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.1.)
  Known gap: This is the specific legal checklist behind the general "habitable" duty stated above — a unit can look fine and still be legally uninhabitable if it's substantially missing even one of these items. This list also includes a locking mail receptacle requirement for residential hotel units specifically, which this document doesn't restate since it isn't relevant to an ordinary residential lease. This is one state's statute; other states define habitability differently, whether by statute, regulation, or case law. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this.

STOVE AND REFRIGERATOR REQUIREMENT
For a lease entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026, a unit is also legally uninhabitable if it substantially lacks a working stove capable of safely generating heat for cooking, or a working refrigerator capable of safely storing food — and a stove or refrigerator under an active manufacturer or public-entity recall doesn't count as safe. Tenant and Landlord can agree at signing that Tenant will bring and maintain their own refrigerator instead, using specific statutory language, but Tenant can end that arrangement with 30 days' written notice, after which Landlord must install a working refrigerator.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "a stove that is maintained in good working order and capable of safely generating heat for cooking purposes. A stove that is subject to a recall by the manufacturer or a public entity is not capable of safely generating heat for cooking purposes. This paragraph shall only apply to a lease entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(10) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, stove requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.1.)
  "a refrigerator that is maintained in good working order and capable of safely storing food. A refrigerator that is subject to recall by the manufacturer or a public entity is not capable of safely storing food."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, refrigerator requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.1.)
  "The lease contains a statement in substantially the following form: “Under state law, the landlord is required to provide a refrigerator in good working order in your unit. By checking this box, you acknowledge that you have asked to bring your own refrigerator and that you are responsible for keeping that refrigerator in working order.”"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(B)(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, required opt-out language for a tenant-supplied refrigerator (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.1.)
  "The lease provides that the tenant may, with 30 days written notice, inform the landlord that they no longer wish to keep their own refrigerator in the unit, and that at the end of the 30-day notice period, the landlord shall install a refrigerator in good working order in the unit."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(B)(ii) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, tenant's right to revert to a landlord-provided refrigerator (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.1.)
  Known gap: This requirement doesn't apply to every kind of housing — it's carved out for permanent supportive housing, single-room-occupancy units, residential hotel units, and housing with shared or communal kitchens (including assisted living facilities), since those housing types often don't work the way an ordinary rental unit does. This is a very new requirement — it only applies to leases entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026 — and it's one state's statute, not a general rule. All four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1941.1) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

LANDLORD'S RIGHT TO ENTER
Landlord may enter the unit only in these specific cases: (1) an emergency; (2) to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, to supply necessary or agreed services, or to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, mortgagee, tenant, worker, or contractor, or to make the pre-move-out inspection described elsewhere in this document; (3) when Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit; or (4) under a court order. (Two further categories exist under separate statutes for specific health, safety, and emergency-preparedness purposes this document doesn't cover.) Except in an emergency or abandonment, entry is limited to normal business hours and generally requires reasonable written notice stating the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry — but written notice itself isn't always required: no notice at all is required if Tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry; oral notice is enough to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, if Landlord has separately given Tenant written notice within the last 120 days that the property is for sale; and Landlord and Tenant may agree orally to a repair or service visit within the coming week, with no written notice required for that agreed visit either. Landlord can't abuse this right of access or use it to harass Tenant.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "A landlord may enter the dwelling unit only in the following cases: (1) In case of emergency. (2) To make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors or to make an inspection pursuant to subdivision (f) of Section 1950.5. (3) When the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises. (4) Pursuant to court order."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the specific permitted purposes for entry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "Except in cases of emergency or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises, entry may not be made during other than normal business hours unless the tenant consents to an entry during other than normal business hours at the time of entry."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, entry limited to normal business hours (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "Except as provided in subdivision (e), or as provided in paragraph (2) or (3), the landlord shall give the tenant reasonable notice in writing of his or her intent to enter and enter only during normal business hours. The notice shall include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, written notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "Twenty-four hours shall be presumed to be reasonable notice in absence of evidence to the contrary."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, 24-hour presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "If the purpose of the entry is to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, the notice may be given orally, in person or by telephone, if the landlord or his or her agent has notified the tenant in writing within 120 days of the oral notice that the property is for sale and that the landlord or agent may contact the tenant orally for the purpose described above."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, oral notice suffices to show the unit to a prospective purchaser (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "The tenant and the landlord may agree orally to an entry to make agreed repairs or supply agreed services. The agreement shall include the date and approximate time of the entry, which shall be within one week of the agreement. In this case, the landlord is not required to provide the tenant a written notice."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, an oral agreement for a repair or service visit needs no written notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "No notice of entry is required under this section: (1) To respond to an emergency. (2) If the tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry. (3) After the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, when no notice at all is required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "The landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, no abuse or harassment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  Known gap: Twenty-four hours' written notice is presumed reasonable, but that's a presumption, not an absolute floor — it can be rebutted by evidence either way. This is one state's statute; notice requirements for landlord entry vary by state. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1954) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

TENANT'S MAINTENANCE RESPONSIBILITIES
Tenant will keep the unit clean and sanitary, use all appliances and fixtures properly, and promptly notify Landlord of any condition needing repair. Tenant is responsible for damage caused by Tenant's own negligence or misuse, beyond ordinary wear and tear.

LATE FEES
If rent is not paid within _______ days of the due date, Tenant will owe a late fee of $_______ (or _______% of the monthly rent).

MEGAN'S LAW DATABASE NOTICE
California Civil Code § 2079.10a requires that every lease or rental agreement for single-family residential real property, and every leasehold interest in multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units, entered into on or after July 1, 1999, contain a statutorily specified notice, in not less than 8-point type. For a lease or rental agreement entered into on or after April 1, 2006, the required notice reads: "Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides." Once this notice has been delivered, the lessor or broker is not required to provide additional information about the proximity of registered sex offenders, and the notice does not give rise to any cause of action against the disclosing party by a registered sex offender.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every lease or rental agreement for single-family residential real property entered into on or after July 1, 1999, any leasehold interest in real property consisting of multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units entered into after that date, and every contract for the sale of residential real property comprised of one to four dwelling units entered into on or after that date, shall contain, in not less than 8-point type, a notice as specified in paragraph (1), (2), or (3)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(a), California Civil Code, scope of the Megan's Law notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.10a.)
  "A contract entered into by the parties on or after April 1, 2006, shall contain the following notice: Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(a)(3), California Civil Code, current required notice text (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.10a.)
  "Subject to subdivision (c), upon delivery of the notice to the lessee or buyer of the real property, the lessor, seller, or broker is not required to provide information in addition to that contained in the notice regarding the proximity of registered sex offenders."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(b), California Civil Code, delivering the notice is deemed adequate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.10a.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's approach to a statewide sex-offender registry notice requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific lease. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.10a); no additional independent source was found for this. This clause states the same statutory notice already verified elsewhere in this corpus for a residential purchase agreement, adapted to lease-specific language, since § 2079.10a's own scope provision expressly covers both leases and sales.

SIGNATURES
Signed:

Landlord: _______________________ Date: _______________
Tenant: _______________________ Date: _______________

—
Groundtruth v1 demo · every "Verified" citation links to a real, checked source.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, advance rent for a longer lease

(2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. expectedJSON.gap: A lease of six months or longer can separately require an advance rent payment of up to six months' rent, on top of the security deposit cap above — a different rule from the deposit cap itself, and easy to conflate with it. This is one state's statute, current as of a 2024 change that lowered the general cap to one month's rent; deposit limits and return deadlines vary by state, and this document doesn't track any state but this one. All six citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Before Tenant moves out, Landlord must notify Tenant in writing of Tenant's option to request an initial (pre-move-out) inspection and the right to be present for it. If Tenant requests one, Landlord must inspect no earlier than two weeks before the move-out date and give Tenant at least 48 hours' written notice of the inspection date and time. The point of this inspection is to let Tenant fix any identified problems before move-out, to avoid a deduction from the deposit for them.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the pre-move-out inspection right
citations.quote: Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. The purpose of the initial inspection shall be to allow the tenant an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies, in a manner consistent with the rights and obligations of the parties under the rental agreement, in order to avoid deductions from the security.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 48-hour inspection notice
citations.quote: The landlord shall give at least 48 hours’ prior written notice of the date and time of the inspection if either a mutual time is agreed upon, or if a mutually agreed time cannot be scheduled but the tenant still wishes an inspection.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, effect of not identifying an issue at the inspection
citations.quote: if an initial inspection is conducted pursuant to this subdivision and, at the time of inspection, the premises do not contain tenant possessions that prevent the landlord from identifying repairs or cleanings due to the presence of those possessions, the landlord shall not use the security for deductions for repairs or cleanings that are not identified in the itemized statement described in paragraph (2).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(7) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, this right doesn't apply to a for-cause unlawful detainer
citations.quote: The requirements of this subdivision do not apply when the tenancy is terminated pursuant to subdivision (2), (3), or (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

expectedJSON.gap: If Tenant requests this inspection and the unit isn't full of Tenant's belongings in a way that would hide problems from view, Landlord generally can't later deduct from the deposit for a repair or cleaning issue that wasn't identified at that inspection. This is a real, concrete consequence of the inspection right, not just a formality — and it's easy to miss because the inspection itself is optional (Tenant has to request it; if Tenant doesn't, this whole process — and its protection — doesn't apply). This entire inspection right doesn't apply at all if the tenancy is ending through an unlawful detainer based on nonpayment of rent, a lease breach, or waste/nuisance — those specific for-cause terminations void the right described in this clause. This is one state's statute; not every state gives tenants this specific right. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: For a tenancy that begins on or after July 1, 2025, Landlord must photograph the unit before or at the start of the tenancy. Separately, beginning April 1, 2025, Landlord must photograph the unit after Tenant moves out but before making any repairs or cleaning charged against the deposit, and again after that repair or cleaning is finished.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, move-in photo requirement
citations.quote: For tenancies that begin on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord shall take photographs of the unit immediately before, or at the inception of, the tenancy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, move-out before-and-after photo requirement
citations.quote: Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord shall take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after the possession of the unit is returned to the landlord, but prior to any repairs or cleanings for which the landlord will make a deduction from or claim against the security deposit pursuant to this section, and shall also take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after such repairs or cleanings are completed.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the photos are a required part of the deduction documentation
citations.quote: If a deduction is made for repairs or cleanings allowed by this section, the landlord shall provide photographs taken pursuant to subdivision (g), along with a written explanation of the cost of the allowable repairs or cleanings, as described in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive.

expectedJSON.gap: This is a very recent requirement — it phases in on two different dates for two different purposes (a baseline record at move-in, and a before-and-after record around any move-out deduction) — and it's one state's statute, not a nationwide practice. The move-out photos aren't just good practice: for any deduction the landlord makes for repairs or cleaning, the statute separately requires the landlord to provide those same photographs to the tenant, along with a written explanation of the cost, as part of the itemized deduction statement — so skipping the photos leaves the landlord unable to fully comply with that separate documentation requirement. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Landlord must maintain the property in a condition fit for human habitation and repair conditions that make it uninhabitable, except for conditions Tenant caused.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, landlord's habitability duty
citations.quote: The lessor of a building intended for the occupation of human beings must, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, put it into a condition fit for such occupation, and repair all subsequent dilapidations thereof, which render it untenantable, except such as are mentioned in section nineteen hundred and twenty-nine.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, habitability duty can't be waived
citations.quote: Any agreement by a lessee of a dwelling waiving or modifying his rights under Section 1941 or 1942 shall be void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable, except that the lessor and the lessee may agree that the lessee shall undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute's own text says this duty applies "in the absence of an agreement to the contrary" — which could read as if a lease could waive it. A separate provision closes that door for residential tenancies: a lease clause waiving or modifying this duty is void as against public policy, for any condition that actually makes the unit uninhabitable. The one thing landlord and tenant can agree to instead is having the tenant handle some repairs or maintenance as part of the rental terms — that's different from waiving the underlying habitability duty altogether. This is one state's statute; habitability protections exist in some form in most states, but the details vary.

expectedJSON.body: A unit is legally uninhabitable if it substantially lacks any of the following: effective weatherproofing (including intact windows and doors); working plumbing and gas fixtures that met the code in effect when installed; hot and cold running water connected to an approved sewage system; working heating that met the code in effect when installed; working electrical wiring and lighting that met the code in effect when installed; a building and grounds kept clean, sanitary, and free of debris, rodents, and vermin; adequate garbage and rubbish receptacles, kept in clean condition and good repair; and floors, stairways, and railings kept in good repair.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(1)-(8) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the specific tenantability checklist
citations.quote: A dwelling shall be deemed untenantable for purposes of Section 1941 if it substantially lacks any of the following affirmative standard characteristics or is a residential unit described in Section 17920.3 or 17920.10 of the Health and Safety Code: (1) Effective waterproofing and weather protection of roof and exterior walls, including unbroken windows and doors. (2) Plumbing or gas facilities that conformed to applicable law in effect at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (3) A water supply approved under applicable law that is under the control of the tenant, capable of producing hot and cold running water, or a system that is under the control of the landlord, that produces hot and cold running water, furnished to appropriate fixtures, and connected to a sewage disposal system approved under applicable law. (4) Heating facilities that conformed with applicable law at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (5) Electrical lighting, with wiring and electrical equipment that conformed with applicable law at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (6) Building, grounds, and appurtenances at the time of the commencement of the lease or rental agreement, and all areas under control of the landlord, kept in every part clean, sanitary, and free from all accumulations of debris, filth, rubbish, garbage, rodents, and vermin. (7) An adequate number of appropriate receptacles for garbage and rubbish, in clean condition and good repair at the time of the commencement of the lease or rental agreement, with the landlord providing appropriate serviceable receptacles thereafter and being responsible for the clean condition and good repair of the receptacles under their control. (8) Floors, stairways, and railings maintained in good repair.

expectedJSON.gap: This is the specific legal checklist behind the general "habitable" duty stated above — a unit can look fine and still be legally uninhabitable if it's substantially missing even one of these items. This list also includes a locking mail receptacle requirement for residential hotel units specifically, which this document doesn't restate since it isn't relevant to an ordinary residential lease. This is one state's statute; other states define habitability differently, whether by statute, regulation, or case law. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: For a lease entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026, a unit is also legally uninhabitable if it substantially lacks a working stove capable of safely generating heat for cooking, or a working refrigerator capable of safely storing food — and a stove or refrigerator under an active manufacturer or public-entity recall doesn't count as safe. Tenant and Landlord can agree at signing that Tenant will bring and maintain their own refrigerator instead, using specific statutory language, but Tenant can end that arrangement with 30 days' written notice, after which Landlord must install a working refrigerator.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(10) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, stove requirement
citations.quote: a stove that is maintained in good working order and capable of safely generating heat for cooking purposes. A stove that is subject to a recall by the manufacturer or a public entity is not capable of safely generating heat for cooking purposes. This paragraph shall only apply to a lease entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, refrigerator requirement
citations.quote: a refrigerator that is maintained in good working order and capable of safely storing food. A refrigerator that is subject to recall by the manufacturer or a public entity is not capable of safely storing food.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(B)(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required opt-out language for a tenant-supplied refrigerator
citations.quote: The lease contains a statement in substantially the following form: “Under state law, the landlord is required to provide a refrigerator in good working order in your unit. By checking this box, you acknowledge that you have asked to bring your own refrigerator and that you are responsible for keeping that refrigerator in working order.”

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(B)(ii) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's right to revert to a landlord-provided refrigerator
citations.quote: The lease provides that the tenant may, with 30 days written notice, inform the landlord that they no longer wish to keep their own refrigerator in the unit, and that at the end of the 30-day notice period, the landlord shall install a refrigerator in good working order in the unit.

expectedJSON.gap: This requirement doesn't apply to every kind of housing — it's carved out for permanent supportive housing, single-room-occupancy units, residential hotel units, and housing with shared or communal kitchens (including assisted living facilities), since those housing types often don't work the way an ordinary rental unit does. This is a very new requirement — it only applies to leases entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026 — and it's one state's statute, not a general rule. All four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1941.1) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Landlord may enter the unit only in these specific cases: (1) an emergency; (2) to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, to supply necessary or agreed services, or to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, mortgagee, tenant, worker, or contractor, or to make the pre-move-out inspection described elsewhere in this document; (3) when Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit; or (4) under a court order. (Two further categories exist under separate statutes for specific health, safety, and emergency-preparedness purposes this document doesn't cover.) Except in an emergency or abandonment, entry is limited to normal business hours and generally requires reasonable written notice stating the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry — but written notice itself isn't always required: no notice at all is required if Tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry; oral notice is enough to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, if Landlord has separately given Tenant written notice within the last 120 days that the property is for sale; and Landlord and Tenant may agree orally to a repair or service visit within the coming week, with no written notice required for that agreed visit either. Landlord can't abuse this right of access or use it to harass Tenant.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the specific permitted purposes for entry
citations.quote: A landlord may enter the dwelling unit only in the following cases: (1) In case of emergency. (2) To make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors or to make an inspection pursuant to subdivision (f) of Section 1950.5. (3) When the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises. (4) Pursuant to court order.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, entry limited to normal business hours
citations.quote: Except in cases of emergency or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises, entry may not be made during other than normal business hours unless the tenant consents to an entry during other than normal business hours at the time of entry.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, written notice requirement
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (e), or as provided in paragraph (2) or (3), the landlord shall give the tenant reasonable notice in writing of his or her intent to enter and enter only during normal business hours. The notice shall include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 24-hour presumption
citations.quote: Twenty-four hours shall be presumed to be reasonable notice in absence of evidence to the contrary.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, oral notice suffices to show the unit to a prospective purchaser
citations.quote: If the purpose of the entry is to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, the notice may be given orally, in person or by telephone, if the landlord or his or her agent has notified the tenant in writing within 120 days of the oral notice that the property is for sale and that the landlord or agent may contact the tenant orally for the purpose described above.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, an oral agreement for a repair or service visit needs no written notice
citations.quote: The tenant and the landlord may agree orally to an entry to make agreed repairs or supply agreed services. The agreement shall include the date and approximate time of the entry, which shall be within one week of the agreement. In this case, the landlord is not required to provide the tenant a written notice.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, when no notice at all is required
citations.quote: No notice of entry is required under this section: (1) To respond to an emergency. (2) If the tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry. (3) After the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no abuse or harassment
citations.quote: The landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

expectedJSON.gap: Twenty-four hours' written notice is presumed reasonable, but that's a presumption, not an absolute floor — it can be rebutted by evidence either way. This is one state's statute; notice requirements for landlord entry vary by state. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1954) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Tenant will keep the unit clean and sanitary, use all appliances and fixtures properly, and promptly notify Landlord of any condition needing repair. Tenant is responsible for damage caused by Tenant's own negligence or misuse, beyond ordinary wear and tear.
If rent is not paid within _______ days of the due date, Tenant will owe a late fee of $_______ (or _______% of the monthly rent).

California Civil Code § 2079.10a requires that every lease or rental agreement for single-family residential real property, and every leasehold interest in multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units, entered into on or after July 1, 1999, contain a statutorily specified notice, in not less than 8-point type. For a lease or rental agreement entered into on or after April 1, 2006, the required notice reads: "Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides." Once this notice has been delivered, the lessor or broker is not required to provide additional information about the proximity of registered sex offenders, and the notice does not give rise to any cause of action against the disclosing party by a registered sex offender.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the Megan's Law notice requirement
citations.quote: Every lease or rental agreement for single-family residential real property entered into on or after July 1, 1999, any leasehold interest in real property consisting of multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units entered into after that date, and every contract for the sale of residential real property comprised of one to four dwelling units entered into on or after that date, shall contain, in not less than 8-point type, a notice as specified in paragraph (1), (2), or (3).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, current required notice text
citations.quote: A contract entered into by the parties on or after April 1, 2006, shall contain the following notice: Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, delivering the notice is deemed adequate
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (c), upon delivery of the notice to the lessee or buyer of the real property, the lessor, seller, or broker is not required to provide information in addition to that contained in the notice regarding the proximity of registered sex offenders.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's approach to a statewide sex-offender registry notice requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific lease. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.10a); no additional independent source was found for this. This clause states the same statutory notice already verified elsewhere in this corpus for a residential purchase agreement, adapted to lease-specific language, since § 2079.10a's own scope provision expressly covers both leases and sales.
